title: Extract Privileged Communications from Production Set — Privilege Log and Clawback Memorandum

blind.coverage: I read all 66 criteria, the instructions, the judge prompt and the solver system prompt. I read all 15 documents in full: flagged batches a–j, the NorthBridge QC report, the clawback order, the engagement letter, the Production 3 cover letter and the grand jury subpoena. I checked the text of FRE 502(b) and 502(d), and the Explanatory Note to 502(d), through a web fetch of the Cornell LII page. That fetch returned a model summary with quotes, not the raw page. A CourtListener search for Third Circuit common-interest authority (Teleglobe) returned nothing, so no case law is cited as verified. Limits: I did not independently research whether a vice president has authority to waive a corporate privilege, or the Third Circuit's dual-purpose work-product standard. Those points are flagged as judgment calls, not verified law.

findings.title: C-062 and C-046 rely on internal DOC_00X labels the solver never sees; the QC report's own numbering is off by two
findings.explanation: The solver sees files named flagged-doc-batch-a..j and a QC report that numbers the documents 1–10. The report puts the Mullins–Nagarajan email at #4, Nagarajan–Metcalf at #6, the Audit Committee email at #8 and the draft policy at #10. The rubric's DOC_003–DOC_012 labels appear nowhere in the record. C-062 says only 'recommends clawback for DOC_006, DOC_008, and DOC_010' and gives no Bates numbers or descriptions. The judge sees only the deliverable and this one criterion, so it cannot tie these labels to the memo's discussion. If the memo follows the QC numbering, the judge may read DOC_006 as item #6 (Metcalf), DOC_008 as #8 and DOC_010 as #10 (the draft policy), which is the wrong set. C-046 lists ten bare DOC labels, so a correct memo that identifies documents by Bates number or QC item number may be failed as incomplete. The QC report also says it lists 'twelve (12) representative documents' but lists only ten. That adds to the confusion.

evidence.quote: PASS if the memo recommends clawback for DOC_006, DOC_008, and DOC_010.
PASS if the memo includes a privilege determination for each of the following documents: DOC_003, DOC_004, DOC_005, DOC_006, DOC_007, DOC_008, DOC_009, DOC_010, DOC_011, and DOC_012.
the following twelve (12) representative documents are identified individually
**6.** --- *Common interest email (Nagarajan--Metcalf)* Bates RDGL-00020512 through RDGL-00020515.

findings.suggested_fix: Add a Bates range and short description after every DOC label in C-046 and C-062, as the other criteria already do. Also fix the QC report's 'twelve' to 'ten'.

findings.title: C-038 assumes Correa had already retained Kendrick Sable by Oct 8, 2023; the record suggests she had not
findings.explanation: C-038 requires the memo to reason that Nagarajan was advising a former employee 'who had already retained separate counsel (Kendrick Sable LLP)'. The record points the other way. Correa's Oct 8, 2023 email says she does not know where to start and turns to Nagarajan as the person she trusts most. Metcalf first appears on Nov 2, 2023, when he introduces himself as her counsel. The only 'now represented' statements are dated December 2023 and February 2024. A careful memo would say Correa had no counsel yet, which actually makes the inadvertent-relationship risk worse. A judge applying C-038 literally may fail that memo for leaving out, or contradicting, the retained-counsel premise.

evidence.quote: a former employee (Correa) who had already retained separate counsel (Kendrick Sable LLP)
I just don't know where to start with something like this, and you're the smartest lawyer I know.
Date: November 2, 2023, 9:17 AM EST ... I am writing in my capacity as counsel to Janet Correa

findings.suggested_fix: Remove 'who had already retained separate counsel (Kendrick Sable LLP)'. Or replace it with 'who was unrepresented at the time and later retained Kendrick Sable LLP'.

findings.title: C-065 assumes DOC_003 is on the privilege log, but the rubric leaves DOC_003's privilege status open
findings.explanation: C-023 and C-024 only require analysis of whether the September 2020 Ellsworth–Nagarajan emails were prospective-client consultations. No criterion requires a conclusion. The record strongly supports a 'not privileged' finding. Ellsworth started the exchange as a networking pitch ('no obligation, of course'). No engagement followed for three years. The engagement letter expressly declines to adopt prior communications. A competent reviewer who concludes DOC_003 is not privileged and leaves it off the log still passes C-058 and C-059 (6-of-8 thresholds). That reviewer fails C-065, because C-065 grades 'the privilege log entry for DOC_003' and there is no entry to grade.

evidence.quote: PASS if the privilege log entry for DOC_003 correctly identifies Catherine Ellsworth (Harwick & Calloway LLP) and Priya Nagarajan (Ridgeline General Counsel) as the communicants.
Nothing in this letter is intended to constitute a retroactive adoption or ratification of any prior communications as falling within the scope of this engagement.
I'd be happy to share some general thoughts on best practices we've seen work well for companies at a similar stage — no obligation, of course.

findings.suggested_fix: Make C-065 conditional: pass if DOC_003 is logged with the correct parties, or is excluded with a stated reason. Or delete C-065.

findings.title: C-017/C-018 treat only messages 9–10 of DOC_005 as privileged, though other messages request or relay legal advice
findings.explanation: Counting oldest-first, message 8 (Correa, July 22) says 'Ray, Tom, can you weigh in on whether we can use this?'. That is a direct request to in-house counsel for legal advice on the Nakamura question. Message 7 (Mullins) adds Viklund 'for visibility' and raises the same question so it can be handled 'the right way'. Message 11 (Mullins, July 26) relays counsel's conclusion ('we'll steer clear of the Nakamura data'). Employees' communications that request legal advice or pass it along internally are commonly protected. A reviewer would often redact the Nakamura paragraphs of messages 7, 8 and 11 as well. C-017 requires the memo to find that 'the remaining 12 messages' are not privileged, and C-018 requires the log to claim only messages 9–10. That fails a careful but slightly broader redaction. The oldest-first numbering is also never stated in the record, which shows the thread newest-first; the content alternative in each criterion reduces that risk.

evidence.quote: only the specific legal exchange (messages 9 and 10 ...) is privileged, while the remaining 12 messages in the thread are not privileged
Good question on the Nakamura study — Ray, Tom, can you weigh in on whether we can use this?
Got it — we'll steer clear of the Nakamura data in the detail aid.

findings.suggested_fix: Pass any answer that confines the privilege claim to the Nakamura legal exchange: messages 9–10, plus optionally the portions of messages 7, 8 and 11 that request or relay the advice. Fail only if the whole thread, or its business content, is claimed.

findings.title: The rubric requires an element-by-element FRE 502(b) analysis though the 502(d) order largely displaces 502(b)
findings.explanation: The clawback order says production does not waive privilege 'regardless of whether such disclosure was inadvertent or intentional' as long as the clawback procedures are followed. It also says that following those procedures satisfies 502(b) 'as a matter of law'. The 502(d) Explanatory Note likewise says such an order may provide for return of documents without waiver irrespective of the care taken by the disclosing party. A strong memo could therefore say the controlling question is the order's 10-business-day notice and its constructive-knowledge Discovery Date, and treat 502(b) only briefly. The five criteria require separate discussion of 502(b)(1), (b)(2) and (b)(3) and of the 7-day gap under 502(b). They fail such a memo, and no criterion credits recognizing that 502(d) displaces 502(b). Many memos would include 502(b) as a backup argument, so this is arguable rather than clearly defective.

evidence.quote: regardless of whether such disclosure was inadvertent or intentional, provided that the Producing Party complies with the clawback procedures set forth in this Order
Compliance with the procedures set forth in this Section IV shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements of Federal Rule of Evidence 502(b) as a matter of law
PASS if the memo addresses FRE 502(b)(1) by explaining that the disclosure was inadvertent

authorities.proposition: A 502(d) order may provide for non-waiver/return of documents irrespective of the care taken by the disclosing party.

findings.suggested_fix: Let an analysis of the order's own non-waiver standard (the 10-business-day notice, the Discovery Date and the diligence duty) satisfy the timeliness, preventive-steps and rectification criteria. Do not require each 502(b) subsection to be named.

findings.title: Four criteria require treating DOC_004's privilege as waived, with no room for the authority-to-waive argument
findings.explanation: Lassiter forwarded the memo against Viklund's express instruction not to share it. Viklund's memo reserves decisions about disclosure to the legal department. Under the Weintraub line of cases, management controls a corporation's privilege, and courts disagree on whether an employee's unauthorized disclosure waives it. Deshmukh is also a paid Ridgeline speaker, which gives at least a weak consultant or functional-equivalent argument. The rubric's view (likely waived, do not claw back) is mainstream and defensible. But a competent memo that asserts privilege as a low-cost protective clawback under the 502(d) order, while flagging the waiver risk, fails four separate criteria. Under the all-pass metric, one judgment call therefore carries four criteria of weight.

evidence.quote: Please do not forward or distribute this analysis outside the legal department without my prior approval.
FAIL if the memo recommends clawing back DOC_004.

authorities.citation: Commodity Futures Trading Comm'n v. Weintraub, 471 U.S. 343 (1985)
authorities.proposition: Power to waive the corporate attorney-client privilege rests with corporate management.

findings.suggested_fix: Merge C-014, C-015 and C-060 into one criterion. Pass memos that find waiver likely and either decline clawback or assert only a protective claim based on the employee's lack of authority, with the risk explained.

findings.title: C-020 describes slides 1–8 as 'predating any litigation threat', but the whole deck was prepared after the CID
findings.explanation: The whole deck was created on Dec 5, 2023, after DOJ's Oct 2 informal contact and the Nov 1 CID. Slide 2 says the deck evaluates exposure 'in connection with recent government interest'. So slides 1–8 did not predate the litigation threat; only their subject matter is routine. Under a 'because of litigation' test, a reviewer could reasonably call at least slide 2, or the whole deck, work product. C-020 fails any answer that treats slides 1–8 as work product. Splitting the deck by portion is the better view, but C-020's factual premise is inaccurate.

evidence.quote: slides 1-8 of DOC_009 (covering routine regulatory risk matters predating any litigation threat) are not protected by the work product doctrine
evaluates the company's exposure in connection with **recent government interest** in the product's promotional practices.

findings.suggested_fix: Rephrase: slides 3–8 cover routine compliance content that would have been prepared in similar form anyway. Accept answers that assert attorney-client privilege over slides 1–8, and do not fail an answer for treating slide 2 as work product.

findings.title: C-050 requires recommending a formal common-interest agreement with Correa despite signs her interests diverge; C-062 calls DOC_008 'clearly privileged'
findings.explanation: The record repeatedly flags that Correa's interests may diverge from Ridgeline's. Viklund's deck says so. The Audit Committee is probing her separation terms and any side letters. DOC_008 itself is about presenting 'a consistent narrative to the government', which could draw scrutiny as witness alignment. A competent memo might advise re-evaluating the coordination, or formalizing it only with conflict-waiver and withdrawal terms, instead of simply signing an agreement. C-050 fails that memo. C-062 also calls DOC_006 and DOC_008 'clearly privileged', which conflicts with C-002 and C-008, where the rubric itself identifies serious weaknesses in those same documents.

evidence.quote: Coordinate with Andrew Metcalf at Kendrick Sable LLP regarding any contact with Janet Correa --- recognize that Ms. Correa's interests may diverge from the company's.
how our respective clients can present a consistent narrative to the government
FAIL if any of these three clearly privileged documents are recommended against clawback.

findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite C-050 to pass any forward-looking recommendation on the common-interest gap: formalize with appropriate protective terms, or reassess the coordination. Drop 'clearly' from C-062.

findings.title: Reply timestamps come before the original emails in DOC_006 and DOC_010; criteria give DOC_006's direction backwards
findings.explanation: In DOC_006, Nagarajan's reply is stamped 03 Aug 2022 02:23 UTC, which is the evening of Aug 2 Eastern time. Mullins's original request is Aug 3 at 10:47 AM, and the reply says she read the deck 'over lunch'. In DOC_010, Pak-Morrison's reply (15 Feb 2024 03:42 UTC) likewise comes before Greenwald's 10:17 AM EST email. A reviewer who converts to local time could log Aug 2 or Feb 14. C-001 and C-005 also describe DOC_006 as a 'Mullins-to-Nagarajan' email, but a log listing the top message would correctly show Nagarajan as author. The Bates identifiers probably let judges match anyway, so the practical impact is low.

evidence.quote: Sent: Wednesday, August 3, 2022 10:47 AM
dated August 3, 2022, from Sandra Mullins to Priya Nagarajan

findings.suggested_fix: Correct the header timestamps. Describe DOC_006 as a Mullins–Nagarajan email chain whose top message is from Nagarajan.

blind.overall: The rubric is detailed and mostly faithful to the record. The case numbers, Bates ranges, dates and the NorthBridge error details all match the documents, and the 6-of-8 thresholds in C-058 and C-059 sensibly allow reasonable exclusions. The most serious defects are mechanical. C-046 and C-062 grade against internal DOC_00X labels that neither the solver nor the judge can map, and the QC report's own numbering is off by two. C-065 assumes DOC_003 is logged even though no criterion requires that result. C-038 includes a fact about Correa's counsel that the record contradicts. On substance, C-017 and C-018 draw the DOC_005 privilege line too narrowly. Several other criteria turn on one defensible position: 502(b) analysis despite a 502(d) order, the DOC_004 waiver (weighted four times), work-product status of slides 1–8, and recommending a common-interest agreement. Under the all-pass metric, these can fail competent answers that take a different reasonable view.

sol_verdicts.reason: Counted oldest-first, batch C's message 8 is Correa's Jul 22 note: 'Ray, Tom, can you weigh in on whether we can use this?' Message 11 is Mullins's Jul 26 reply: 'we'll steer clear of the Nakamura data.' Those passages ask for and relay the legal advice. C-017's PASS requires finding 'the remaining 12 messages' not privileged, so a broader partial redaction falls between its PASS and FAIL conditions. C-018's FAIL applies only to a whole-thread claim, so it is softer. C-016 only asks the memo to recognise that the thread is mixed, and a broader redaction still does that.

The deck divides itself: slide 2 labels Part I (slides 3–8) 'Routine regulatory compliance posture'. The QC report codes it 'Work Product (Partial)'. So the split in C-019 and C-022 has support in the record. C-020's premise that slides 1–8 were 'predating any litigation threat' is false: the whole deck was created Dec 5, 2023, after the CID, and slide 8 is dated 'as of November 30, 2023'. The rubric's conclusion is defensible, but a reasoned claim over the whole deck, or over slides 1–2, could fail. That makes C-020 arguable, not confirmed.

In DOC_011 (Oct 8, 2023), Correa says she does not know where to start and turns to Nagarajan. Metcalf first appears as her counsel on Nov 2, 2023 (batch F). Nothing in the record shows she had retained Kendrick Sable by Oct 8. C-038 builds that unsupported fact into its PASS condition.

Clawback Order IV.B.2(iv) requires the Clawback Notice to be 'accompanied by, or followed within five (5) business days by, a privilege log entry for each document'. The log is therefore served on AUSA Cooperman. C-006 and C-012 require log entries that admit crime-fraud and common-interest weaknesses, which contradicts C-004's own warning against conceding substance. A competent log ready for service, with the risks kept in the memo, fails both. C-004 is itself sound.

The record contains no written agreement, and Nagarajan proposes only to 'formalize coordination' later. Saying the absence 'weakens' protection is a fair practical point, not a claim that a writing is legally required, so C-008, C-010 and C-049 are sound. C-012 fails for the served-log reason given above. C-050 requires recommending an agreement even though the record flags that Correa's interests may diverge. A memo that recommends reassessing the coordination instead could fail.

The 502(d) order makes a clawback cheap and preserves the government's right to challenge it, so asserting privilege over DOC_006 and DOC_008 while flagging the risks is the mainstream course. C-003 and C-009 are reasonable. Calling these documents 'clearly privileged' in C-062 overstates it. C-062's larger problem is that it names bare DOC_006/008/010 labels the judge cannot map; the QC report numbers the same documents #4, #6 and #8.

The order protects disclosures 'regardless of whether such disclosure was inadvertent or intentional' and deems compliance with its procedures to satisfy 502(b). The criteria tied to 502(b) subsections can therefore fail a memo built around the order. C-027 (promptness) and C-029/C-030 (the order and its 10-business-day deadline) track the order itself and are sound.

Waiver through voluntary disclosure to an outside KOL is the mainstream view. But Viklund's memo said 'do not forward... without my prior approval'. That supports an argument that the employee had no authority to waive, and a protective clawback under the 502(d) order is a defensible choice. Four criteria all turn on this one judgment call.

findings.title: C-006/C-012 require the served privilege log to admit crime-fraud and common-interest weaknesses, contrary to C-004
findings.explanation: Clawback Order IV.B.2(iv) requires the Clawback Notice to be accompanied or quickly followed by a privilege log entry for each document that complies with the Local Civil Rules. The log for clawback candidates is therefore a document served on AUSA Cooperman. The order asks the log for a basis and identifying facts, not an admission of weaknesses. C-004 itself warns against language that would concede substance to the government. A competent practitioner would keep the crime-fraud and common-interest risks in the internal memo and leave them out of the served log. That answer fails C-006 and C-012. Only an internal working log with a risk column passes. The instructions never say the log is internal.

evidence.quote: Be accompanied by, or followed within five (5) business days by, a privilege log entry for each document that conforms to the requirements of the Local Civil Rules

findings.title: C-065 assumes DOC_003 is logged, but no criterion requires that conclusion

final.changes_from_blind: Added one finding from Sol (O4, C-006/C-012). I checked the Clawback Order: IV.B.2(iv) requires a privilege log entry to accompany the Clawback Notice, so the log is served on the government. Criteria that require the log to admit weaknesses conflict with C-004 and with ordinary practice. Downgraded C-065 (blind O3) from problematic to arguable. Batch A shows Nagarajan 'evaluating whether it makes sense to bring in outside regulatory counsel', so logging DOC_003 is defensible and probably the majority course, and C-065 misgrades only reviewers who exclude it. Split C-018 out as arguable within the DOC_005 finding, because its FAIL condition covers only whole-thread claims. Added C-026 to the 502(b) finding.
